{{short description|Japanese mathematician}}
'''Toshiki Mabuchi''' ([[kanji]]: 満渕俊樹, [[hiragana]]: マブチ トシキ, Mabuchi Toshiki, born in 1950) is a Japanese mathematician, specializing in [[Differential geometry|complex differential geometry]] and [[algebraic geometry]].<ref name=J-Global>{{cite web|website=J-Global – Japan Science and Technology Agency|title=Mabuchi Toshiki|url=https://jglobal.jst.go.jp/en/detail/?JGLOBAL_ID=200901035322362834&t=1}}</ref> In 2006 in Madrid he was an invited speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]].<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Mabuchi, Toshiki|title=Extremal metrics and stabilities on polarized manifolds|year=2006|eprint=math/0603493 }} (published in vol. 2 of the Proceedings of the ICM, Madrid 2006, pages 813–826)</ref> Mabuchi is known for introducing the [[Mabuchi functional]].

== Education and career ==
In 1972 Mabuchi graduated from the University of Tokyo Faculty of Science<ref name=J-Global /> and became a graduate student in mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Mabuchi, Toshiki|title=Remembering Professor Shoshichi Kobayashi|date=July 25, 2013|url=http://www.shoshichikobayashi.com/2013/07/25/remembering-professor-shoshichi-kobayashi-prof-toshiki-mabuchi/}} (translated form the original Japanese by Hisashi Kobayashi)</ref> There he graduated with a Ph.D. in 1977 with thesis ''C3-Actions and Algebraic Threefolds with Ample Tangent Bundle'' and advisor [[Shoshichi Kobayashi]]<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=32024|name=Toshiki Mabuchi}}</ref> As a postdoc Mabuchi was from 1977 to 1978 a guest researcher at the University of Bonn. Since 1978 he is a faculty member of the Department of Mathematics of [[Osaka University]]. His research deals with complex differential geometry, extremal [[Kähler metric]]s, [[K-stability|stability of algebraic varieties]], and the [[Hitchin–Kobayashi correspondence]].<ref name=J-Global />

In 2006 Toshiki Mabuchi and Takashi Shioya received the [[Geometry prize|Geometry Prize of the Mathematical Society of Japan]].

== Research contributions ==
Mabuchi is well-known for his introduction, in 1986, of the ''[[Mabuchi functional|Mabuchi energy]]'', which gives a variational interpretation to the problem of [[Constant scalar curvature Kähler metric|Kähler metrics of constant scalar curvature]]. In particular, the Mabuchi energy is a real-valued function on a Kähler class whose [[Euler-Lagrange equation]] is the constant scalar curvature equation. In the case that the Kähler class represents the first [[Chern class]] of the complex manifold, one has a relation to the [[Kähler-Einstein metric|Kähler-Einstein problem]], due to the fact that constant scalar curvature metrics in such a Kähler class must be Kähler-Einstein.

Owing to the second variation formulas for the Mabuchi energy, every critical point is stable. Furthermore, if one integrates a holomorphic vector field and pulls back a given Kähler metric by the corresponding one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms, then the corresponding restriction of the Mabuchi energy is a linear function of one real variable; its derivative is the ''Futaki invariant'' discovered a few years earlier by Akito Futaki.<ref>A. Futaki. ''An obstruction to the existence of Einstein Kähler metrics.'' Invent. Math. 73 (1983), no. 3, 437–443.</ref> The Futaki invariant and Mabuchi energy are fundamental in understanding obstructions to the existence of Kähler metrics which are Einstein or which have constant scalar curvature.

A year later, by use of the {{math|∂{{overline|∂}}}}-lemma, Mabuchi considered a natural [[Riemannian metric]] on a Kähler class, which allowed him to define length, [[geodesic]]s, and [[curvature]]; the [[sectional curvature]] of Mabuchi's metric is nonpositive. Along geodesics in the Kähler class, the Mabuchi energy is convex. So the Mabuchi energy has strong variational properties.
